title: Baptism, deeper
hookLine: some say baptism brings new birth; others that it signs a birth already happened

lines: HOW CAN A MAN BE BORN WHEN OLD?
cards: It's night, and a respected teacher named Nicodemus has come to find Jesus quietly. He opens politely. Jesus skips the politeness and says a man must be born again to see the kingdom of God.
Nicodemus is baffled, and says so: "How can a man be born when he is old?" Climb back into your mother? Jesus answers with two elements: water and Spirit.
Since then, water has been poured over infants at stone fonts, and grown adults have gone under in rivers. Day one hundred fifty-two met baptism two ways. Today, deeper: what does the water do?

teach.h: BORN OF WATER AND OF THE SPIRIT.
teach.b: The answer: "Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God." Churches across the traditions baptize; the question is what the water does.
One answer: baptism is God's own act, and in it God gives the new birth.

teach.h: GOD'S ACT: THE WASHING OF REGENERATION.
teach.b: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican teaching point to Paul's phrase to Titus, "the washing of regeneration," and read it as describing the font itself. That's one reason these churches baptize infants.
A baby can't decide anything, and in their teaching that's the point: the gift comes first, and faith grows up inside it.

teach.h: A SIGN OF A BIRTH ALREADY GIVEN.
teach.b: A second answer: baptism is an outward sign of a new birth God gives by the Spirit through faith.
Baptist and other believers' churches teach that a person is born again by trusting Christ, then baptized, usually by full immersion, as a public witness that it has already happened.
So they baptize those old enough to say so.

Presbyterian and Reformed churches take a third road: they baptize the infants of believers as a sign and seal of God's covenant promise, while teaching that the water doesn't work automatically. Now what they share.

teach.h: BURIED WITH HIM, RAISED TO NEW LIFE.
teach.b: Paul, to the Romans: "we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life." Under the water, a burial.
Out of it, a rising. Either way, the shape is the same: going down, and coming up, new.

how: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Reformed churches baptize infants as well as adults, by pouring, sprinkling or immersion; Baptist and other believers' churches baptize people who profess faith, usually by full immersion.

o: a washing in water, read as new birth or as its sign
a naming ceremony held when a baby is born
a yearly bath of cleansing before Easter

games.q: you're Nicodemus. Jesus has just told you that you must be born again. what do you say?
o: "how can a man be born when he is old?"
games.why: he asks the obvious question out loud, and Jesus answers: "born of water and of the Spirit."

practice: If you were baptized, bring it to mind, even if only from a photo or a story. If you weren't, bring to mind a beginning that mattered, a moment you went under in some way and came up different.
Notice what in it was given to you, and what you chose. If you pray, give thanks for that beginning; if you don't, just rest in having begun.

wordCard.voice: Baptism. Being washed, buried and raised in water: for some churches the new birth itself, for others its sign.

orig.note: Greek: to dip, to immerse, to wash — the verb behind "baptize."

carryVoice: Your line: born of water. A burial, and a rising. Until tomorrow.
